title: An augmented Lagrangian filter method
contribution: Replaces the forcing sequences of bound-constrained augmented Lagrangian methods by a filter on constraint violation and Lagrangian first-order error, adds restoration switching, an optional penalty estimate and EQP step, proves convergence to KKT/FJ points or infeasibility minimizers, and reports preliminary CUTEst results competitive with SQP solvers.
problem_entry: Interior-point methods cannot warm-start for the thousands of related NLPs in MINLP, active-set methods do not scale to multicore; AL methods could do both but rely on forcing sequences (pp. 2-3); infeasible NLPs are frequent inside MINLP (p. 7).
key_idea: Filter on (eta, omega_0) of the Lagrangian, checkable inside the AL inner solve because the Lagrangian gradient after the multiplier update equals the AL gradient (pp. 4-5, (2.8)); restoration switching conditions (3.15)-(3.16) (pp. 7-8); optional penalty estimate (3.14) and EQP step (pp. 6-7, 9).
assumptions: A1 f, c twice continuously differentiable; A2 ||c(x)|| -> infinity as ||x|| -> infinity, replaceable by finite bounds (pp. 10-11); no bounded-multiplier assumption (p. 5); LICQ only at limits with unbounded penalty (p. 13); analysis without the EQP step (p. 10).
proof_devices: Compactness from the filter's upper bound U on eta (Lemma 4.1, p. 11)
Filter-free neighbourhood of the origin from the sloping envelope (Lemma 4.2, p. 11)
Finite inner loop: sufficient reduction (3.18) would make the AL unbounded below (Lemma 4.3, pp. 11-12)
Inner-to-outer sufficient reduction via the multiplier update, c^T y bounded by a geometric series in beta from filter acceptance (Lemma 4.5, (4.21)-(4.22), pp. 12-13)
Unbounded-penalty case via an external AL theorem (Lemma 4.6, p. 13); three-outcome Theorem 4.1 (p. 13)
experiments: Preliminary C++ filter-al (L-BFGS-B + BQPD) on 429 small CUTEst problems vs filterSQP, SNOPT, MINOS, IPOPT, LANCELOT, metered by function evaluations with performance profiles; 34 failures classified (IEEE evaluation errors vs L-BFGS-B failures) (pp. 14-17, Table 1).
positioning: Extends the AL filter for QPs [44] to NLP; contrasted with AL-then-crossover approaches [13], which it claims to integrate more naturally (p. 4); classical forcing-sequence AL (LANCELOT, ALGENCAN) as the baseline design (p. 3).
writing: Outline deliberately vague first, then detailed components (p. 5); claims bounded to 'competitive' and 'preliminary' (pp. 15, 17); open conjecture stated as a remark (Remark 4.1, p. 14).
limits_future: Implementation preliminary, L-BFGS-B inflates evaluation counts (p. 15); no second-order convergence proof, expected via second-order corrections or a nonmonotone filter (p. 17); MPEC conjecture on bounded penalties untested (p. 14).

method_links.note: Filter globalization carried from SQP into augmented Lagrangian methods, motivated by MINLP warm starts
Evaluation count chosen and justified as meter; failures kept and classified by cause

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Prove the plain core, keep accelerators optional and harmless
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Analysis concentrates on the plain AL method; the penalty heuristic is shown bounded so it does not harm the algorithm; the EQP line search can fall back to the acceptable point

transferable: Analyse the plain algorithm; for each optional heuristic give the single property that keeps the theory intact (bounded estimate, fallback to an acceptable point) (pp. 6, 9)
Turn inner sufficient decrease into outer decrease by subtracting rho||c||^2 and absorbing it once feasibility is shown (p. 12)
Separate failures outside the solver's control (IEEE evaluation errors) from subproblem-solver failures in the failure table (p. 15)

quotes.text: The Achilles’ heel of interior-point methods is the lack of efficient warm-start strategies.
In practice, many NLPs are not feasible; this situation happens frequently, for example during the resolution of MINLPs.

title: Solving Combinatorial Optimization Problems on Quantum Computers
contribution: SIAM News overview that recasts QAOA in optimization terms (Boolean objective as a diagonal operator, combinatorial problem replaced by nonconvex parameter optimization) and lists the obstacles to understanding and realizing its potential, concluding it cannot compete classically until hundreds of high-fidelity qubits exist.
problem_entry: No demonstrably faster quantum algorithm exists for combinatorial optimization; QAOA is the candidate; aim to separate hype from reality (p. 1).
key_idea: Indicator/projector expansion turns f on {0,1}^n into a diagonal operator; QAOA replaces the combinatorial search by a nonconvex optimization over (beta, gamma) solved classically (pp. 1-2).
assumptions: n/a (no theorem); gate counts assume full connectivity and CNOT as native gate (p. 2).
experiments: none; one p = 1 MAXCUT landscape figure on an 8-node graph (p. 1, Fig. 1).
positioning: Cites Hastings and the Goemans-Williamson symmetry result as upper bounds on QAOA; criticizes single local runs in QAOA packages, names multistart and learning approaches (p. 2).
writing: Explicit hype-versus-reality framing (p. 1); obstacles split into understanding and realization (p. 2); opinion flagged as 'In our opinion' on ion traps (p. 2).
limits_future: Parameter optimization for QAOA is 'largely an open question'; hardware with hundreds of qubits needed (p. 2).

method_links.note: Quantum object recast into the home class: combinatorial problem replaced by nonconvex continuous optimization over circuit parameters
Calibrated claim with a stated threshold (hundreds of qubits) and the classical baseline named

transferable: For a hyped method, split obstacles into understanding vs realizing its potential and give a concrete threshold for when it could compete (p. 2)
coauthors: Yuri Alexeev, Jeffrey Larson, Ruslan Shaydulin

quotes.text: To disentangle the hype from reality, we first recap the mathematics of quantum computation and QAOA.
Therefore, until quantum hardware with hundreds of qubits is accessible, QAOA will not be able to compete with classical state-of-the-art methods under the current approach.

contribution: SIAM News summary of the SIAM Climate Task Force report (chaired by Leyffer): recommendations in four areas (climate prediction, resilient communities and environmental justice, clean energy innovation, workforce development) and cross-agency coordination.
problem_entry: How applied mathematics and computational science can support climate science and mitigation; report for Congress and federal agencies (p. 1).
key_idea: Four recommendation areas plus recurring cross-agency coordination (p. 1).
positioning: Aligns its recommendations with the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (p. 1).
writing: Committee report voice; bullet subsets per area (p. 1).
limits_future: Details deferred to the full task force report (not read) (p. 1).

quotes.text: All three authors were members of the SIAM Climate Task Force, with Leyffer acting as chair.

title: Apprentice for event generator tuning
contribution: Describes the open-source tool apprentice for Monte Carlo event generator tuning: pole-free rational surrogates, a choice of chi-square minimizers with multistart, and automatic observable weighting by bilevel or single-level robust optimization, demonstrated on dark-matter limit setting and the ATLAS A14 tune.
problem_entry: Professor's polynomial surrogates fail on ~1/x behaviour, its minimizer suite is limited and untested, and observable weights are tuned by hand (p. 2).
key_idea: Rational surrogates (Stieltjes fit, constrained pole-free fit, linear-denominator case via LP duality) (p. 2); weights by bilevel optimization with an RBF-approximated merit or by a single-level robust formulation using interval endpoints and a coverage constraint (p. 3).
assumptions: Experiment and simulation as independent random variables with mean R_b (p. 3); pole-free guarantee for box domains (p. 2).
experiments: Dark-matter likelihood: rational (4,4) vs polynomial degree 7 with matched coefficient counts, ~30,000 evaluations, ~50x faster than full simulation (p. 6); ATLAS A14 retune vs expert and equal weights by observable class (p. 7, Fig. 2).
positioning: Successor to Professor [1], 'sufficiently different from its predecessor to have its own name' (p. 2).
writing: Tool paper with usage sections and script arguments (pp. 4-6); invitation to contribute via GitHub (pp. 7-8).
limits_future: Future: derivative-free tuning on generator data, chi-square minimizers robust to local minima, ML for dimension reduction and weighting (p. 7).

method_links.note: Surrogate constrained to be pole-free so that downstream optimization problems are well defined
Weighting methods compared by observable class as trade-offs, no single winner
Robust and bilevel optimization formulations carried into generator tuning (weak)

title: Practical algorithms for multivariate rational approximation
contribution: Two methods for multivariate rational least-squares surrogates: a Stieltjes-orthogonalized linear-algebra fit with degree reduction, and a pole-free fit posed as a linear semi-infinite least-squares problem solved by Polyak's outer approximation with multistart pole detection; plus a face-and-interior sampling design and a HEP likelihood application.
problem_entry: Expensive HEP simulations need surrogates; polynomials cannot capture poles, rational fits are fragile with spurious poles that make the downstream objective unbounded (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Linearized fit min sum (p(x_k) - f_k q(x_k))^2; degree reduction while the smallest singular value is negligible (pp. 9-10); 'no poles in D' replaced by q(x) >= tau on D and handled by outer approximation with a global check of min q (pp. 11-13, Algorithm 4.1).
assumptions: Sample points a set of linear independence (p. 5); D a box; degrees fixed in advance (p. 14); no true poles in the sampled domain (p. 23).
proof_devices: Rank count showing W has a zero singular value in the interpolation case (p. 5)
experiments: Analytic test functions, degrees (5,5), K = 2(alpha(M)+alpha(N)), five seeds, noise 0/1e-6/1e-2, held-out L2 error and pole-like points; SG vs LHS vs d-LHD; CPU split fit/multistart; HEP likelihood 288 s vs 14,594 s at ~29,500 evaluations (pp. 13-26, Tables 3-4); multistart vs BARON at equal time (p. 33).
positioning: Extends univariate linearized methods [8, 9, 16] to scattered multivariate data (p. 4); AAA set aside as univariate only (p. 2); outer approximation due to Polyak (p. 11).
writing: Key idea stated in italics as a one-line rule (p. 9); claims bounded by explicit assumptions (p. 23).
limits_future: Degree selection open, harder with noise (p. 27); multistart cost exponential in degrees of freedom (p. 23); tested up to 7 parameters, scalability open; other structural constraints such as monotonicity (p. 28).

method_links.note: Outer approximation carried from MINLP into surrogate fitting for a semi-infinite constraint
Formulation changed (pole-free constraint, open condition made closed) so the downstream optimization is well posed
Cost of the expensive method decomposed and reported; equal-time comparison with BARON; claims bounded by the no-true-pole assumption

transferable: Turn an open 'never zero' requirement into a closed sign-and-margin constraint before optimizing (p. 11)

coauthors: Anthony P. Austin, Mohan Krishnamoorthy, Stephen Mrenna, Juliane Müller, Holger Schulz

quotes.text: The key idea is this: If there are many approximations that will work, one should use the approximation with the lowest-degree denominator.

title: Joint ptycho-tomography with deep generative priors
contribution: ADMM framework for joint ptycho-tomography with a plug-and-play GAN denoiser under a Poisson model, with a denoiser-weight schedule that improves reconstructions of under-sampled noisy simulated data.
problem_entry: Sequential phase retrieval then tomography needs large probe overlap; PnP denoisers are designed for Gaussian noise in linear problems, unlike the nonconvex Poisson ptycho-tomography problem (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: AL/ADMM splitting into ptychography, tomography and regularization subproblems (p. 6); regularization replaced by TomoGAN via PnP (p. 7); blended denoiser step with weight alpha_k (p. 10, Algorithm 1).
assumptions: Poisson MAP model (p. 5); implicit prior without explicit objective, so no formal optimization guarantee (p. 3).
experiments: Two simulated 3D objects, three photon-count noise levels, 50% vs 25% overlap, 250 ADMM iterations with 4 inner CG steps; ML vs TV-MAP vs PnP-GAN by PSNR; six alpha schedules with primal/dual residual decay (pp. 10-16).
positioning: Builds on the authors' ADMM framework [2] and TV work [36]; PnP from Venkatakrishnan et al. [49]; compared with offline denoising and TV (pp. 3-4).
writing: Empirical section explicitly disclaims optimality of the parameter (p. 14).
limits_future: Alpha schedule empirical; code not optimized; only synthetic data because no dedicated beamline exists yet (pp. 14, 16-17).

method_links.note: AL/ADMM toolkit carried into imaging but with an implicit learned prior and no convergence guarantee, against Taste 3; Leyffer fifth of six authors, weak evidence

transferable: Ramp a learned denoiser's weight inside ADMM and judge schedules by both image quality and primal/dual residual decay (pp. 15-16)
coauthors: Selin Aslan, Zhengchun Liu, Viktor Nikitin, Tekin Bicer, Doğa Gürsoy

quotes.text: Our results show that our optimizations can decrease the total number of required projections (with significantly fewer overlapped regions) by 75% compared with using adequately sampled data (based on Nyquist) while maintaining good image quality.
The goal of this section is not to provide an optimal denoiser parameter, but to share valuable observations to decide on an effective one.

title: Inversion of convection-diffusion equation with discrete sources
contribution: Formulates source inversion for convection-diffusion as a large convex-objective binary MIPDECO, shows state-of-the-art MINLP solvers and naive rounding fail, and proposes physics-aware rounding (objective-gap-reduction, mass-preserving) followed by a Hamming-distance trust-region improvement solved as a knapsack, with open Julia and AMPL code.
problem_entry: Identify number and location of pollutant sources from sparse sensors; a test of whether state-of-the-art MINLP solvers can handle MIPDECO (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Eliminate states with the factorized stiffness matrix (p. 12); rounding using the relaxation's objective or mass (pp. 13-15); l1 trust region on binaries = cardinality limit on flips, linear subproblem solved by sorting after sign cases and complementing (pp. 15-18).
assumptions: Linear steady PDE with nonsingular stiffness matrix (p. 12); iid Gaussian noise with known sigma (p. 10); TV regularization with alpha from the L-curve (pp. 10, 20).
proof_devices: Finite termination of the trust-region heuristic: bounded objective, finitely many binary points, integer radius with floor (p. 17)
Mass-preserving rounding keeps the mass difference below 1 (p. 15)
Knapsack reduction by sign case analysis and variable complementing (pp. 17-18)
experiments: 2D finite-difference AMPL instances 16x8 to 256x128 on SCIP, Bonmin (BnB, Hyb, OA), Minotaur (BnB, QG) with 10 CPU-hours, nodes/bounds/gaps/IoU (pp. 20-24, Table 2); rounding schemes by objective, time, PDE solves (Table 3, p. 24); trust region from each rounding in 2D and 3D (pp. 25-30, Table 4).
positioning: Relates to sum-up rounding/CIA, penalty methods and the trust-region steepest-descent method of Hahn et al., called closely related (pp. 8-9); feasibility pump judged impractical for MIPDECO (p. 13).
writing: Negative result first (solvers and naive rounding fail), then the heuristic (pp. 3, 5); referee question reported in the conclusion (p. 31).
limits_future: No optimality guarantee; neighbourhood variant cannot recover missed sources (p. 27); generalization to large MINLPs with convex objective and linear constraints open because states may not be eliminable (p. 31); IPOPT could reuse stiffness factorizations (p. 31).

method_links.note: Solver logs read: SCIP presolve adds 8,002 quadratic constraints though the problem is a bound-constrained NLP after eliminating states; Bonmin-OA returns only W = 0; IPOPT restoration failure
Self-contained finite-difference AMPL instances and Julia code released for reproducibility and solver experimentation
Per-solver bounds and gaps, OA exclusion explained, time limit raised from 2 to 10 hours without change
Diagnosis that general solvers refactor the stiffness matrix every iteration; reusing one factorization makes the heuristic cheap

title: Convergence of sum-up rounding schemes for cloaking problems governed by the Helmholtz equation
contribution: Shows, for a Helmholtz cloaking MIPDECO with finitely many material values, that locally solving refined continuous relaxations and applying multidimensional sum-up rounding on order-conserving grids yields discrete controls whose objective values converge to those of the relaxation (weak* control convergence, norm state convergence), validated numerically with median filtering as a heuristic post-process.
problem_entry: Cloak design treated before as topology optimization with fractional material [18]; the MIPDECO view seeks discrete-valued controls, possibly only an infimum (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Algorithm 1: refine and locally solve the relaxation, refine the rounding grid, apply O(N) SUR along a space-filling-curve order, median-filter (pp. 5, 12-15).
assumptions: Wave number k0 sufficiently small (pp. 16-17, 19); domain regularity (Assumption 2.1, p. 6); order-conserving domain dissection with regular shrinkage (Definition 4.1, pp. 13-14); consistent relaxed controls (p. 14).
proof_devices: Weak* convergence of SUR controls in L-infinity from [28] (Proposition 4.4, p. 15)
Complete continuity of the control-to-state operator from compactness of the Helmholtz solution operator (Lemmas 4.6, 4.9, pp. 16, 18)
Infimum of (P) equals minimum of (R) with a minimizing sequence of discrete controls (Theorem 4.7, p. 17)
Objective convergence of the algorithm's rounded iterates (Theorem 4.11, p. 19)
experiments: FEniCS/dolfin-adjoint/PETSc-Tao, Robin boundary, nine refinements to 2^9 x 2^9 cells (~12 h laptop), state errors and objective gaps for relaxed/SUR/filtered controls (pp. 20-22, Tables 1-2); wave-number sweep 0.24pi-750pi with convergence only for small k0 (p. 23).
positioning: Takes the MIPDECO view against the topology-optimization treatment [18]; builds on Manns-Kirches multidimensional SUR [28]; digitizes [18]'s design to show results are not directly comparable (pp. 3-4, 12, 20-21).
writing: Limitations (chattering, heuristic filtering, no minimizer) stated already in the introduction (p. 5).
limits_future: Chattering unavoidable when the limit is fractional (p. 5); median filter has no guarantee and a counterexample exists (p. 19); proofs only for small k0 (p. 23); future: L1/multi-bang/BV regularization to promote discrete values (pp. 19-20).

method_links.note: Combinatorial integral approximation from mixed-integer optimal control carried into PDE cloaking design; MIPDECO view vs topology optimization

Carried-in assumption (small k0 for unique solvability) checked numerically; method fails beyond it, matching the stated limitation
